questions: How does opening in real London around 1900 change the feel compared with fantasy that starts in another world?
What does it tell us about Digory that Polly first sees him crying about his mother?

questions: Uncle Andrew says people with secret knowledge are free from ordinary rules. Have you met anyone who reasons that way?
He broke a promise to his dying godmother to destroy the box. Does that change how you see him?
Is he a scary villain, a comic one, or both?
Would you have gone after Polly?
chapterQuestions.title: Digory and His Uncle

questions: The wood makes them so content they nearly forget who they are. Peaceful or creepy?
What other in-between places, real or fictional, does it remind you of?
What does Polly's insistence on marking the pool home say about her compared with Digory?
How does Lewis's version of many worlds compare with modern multiverse stories?
chapterQuestions.title: The Wood Between the Worlds

questions: Which details made Charn feel most real to you?
What is Lewis saying with faces that start kind and grow crueler down the line?
The verse dares the reader to strike or wonder forever. Is curiosity a good enough reason to take a risk?
Digory hurts Polly to get his way. Does that change how you feel about him as the hero?
chapterQuestions.title: The Bell and the Hammer

questions: What makes the Queen frightening beyond her power?
She uses almost the same excuse as Uncle Andrew. Why do you think Lewis echoed it on purpose?
She quickly decides whoever sent the children must be a powerful magician. What does that show about how she sees the world?
Who is to blame for bringing her along: Digory, Uncle Andrew, or both?

context.detail: Published in 1955 as the sixth Narnia book, but it takes place before all the others. Lewis finished it in 1954.
context.title: Written late, set first

context.detail: In 1957 Lewis told a young fan, Laurence Krieg, he leaned toward reading the books in story order. HarperCollins later renumbered the series to put this book first.
context.title: The reading-order fight

context.detail: Lewis's mother died of cancer when he was a boy, and many readers see that loss in Digory's sick mother.
context.title: A real loss behind Digory's grief

context.detail: The opening mentions Sherlock Holmes and Nesbit's Bastable children. Her 1906 book The Story of the Amulet follows a strikingly similar pattern.
context.title: A nod to E. Nesbit

guide.lead: In five chapters, a London attic adventure turns into a trip to a dead world, and the children bring back the most dangerous person in it.

recap.summary: London, around 1900. Polly meets Digory, who is staying with Uncle Andrew and Aunt Letty while his mother is seriously ill. They crawl through the attic tunnel, end up in Uncle Andrew's study, and he tricks Polly into touching a yellow ring. She vanishes.
recap.title: The Wrong Door

recap.summary: Uncle Andrew explains the rings came from dust out of Atlantis, in a box he promised his godmother to destroy. Too scared to test them himself, he pressures Digory into following Polly with green rings.
recap.title: Digory and His Uncle

recap.summary: Digory finds Polly in a sleepy wood full of pools. They nearly forget who they are, work out that the wood is an in-between place, mark the pool home, and try another.
recap.title: The Wood Between the Worlds

recap.summary: In Charn, a ruined city under a dying red sun, they find a hall of seated royals and a bell with a verse daring them to strike it. Digory hurts Polly to stop her and rings it. A terrifying queen wakes.
recap.title: The Bell and the Hammer

recap.summary: The Queen explains she destroyed every living thing in her world with one word to win a war against her sister. She plans to rule the children's world, and grabs hold as they escape.
recap.title: The Deplorable Word

guide.spoilerNote: Digory grows up to be someone the Pevensie children meet, and the Queen is a character Narnia fans already know. Ask the group before going here.

themes.prompt: Both believe they live by different rules than ordinary people. Is Uncle Andrew a small, cowardly version of her?

themes.prompt: Guinea pigs, then Polly, then Digory. What does the book say about treating people as means to an end?

themes.prompt: How might Digory's fear for his mother be shaping his choices, including the bell?
themes.title: Grief under the surface

themes.prompt: They argue, compete, and he hurts her. Is it a realistic kid friendship? How does it hold up today?
themes.title: Polly and Digory's friendship

themes.prompt: Written in the shadow of the atomic bomb, the Deplorable Word reads to many as a world-ending weapon. Does that work for you?
themes.title: A dead world as a warning

themes.prompt: Lewis often talks straight to the reader. Charming, or does it pull you out of the story?
themes.title: The narrator's voice

recap.title: The Beginning of Uncle Andrew's Troubles
recap.summary: Back in London, Digory and Polly talk through their fight over the bell and make up. Uncle Andrew, scared but dazzled by the Queen, dresses up and tries to borrow money from Aunt Letty. The Queen bursts in and orders him to take her into the city.

recap.title: What Happened at the Front Door
recap.summary: Aunt Letty is no match for the Queen, whose magic doesn't work in our world but whose strength does. Digory waits at the door with the rings, hoping to send her home. She returns standing on a runaway hansom cab, with a battered Uncle Andrew, a robbed shopkeeper, police and a crowd behind her.

recap.title: The Fight at the Lamp-Post
recap.summary: The Queen tears an iron bar off a lamp-post and fights the crowd. Digory grabs her ankle, and the rings pull her, Uncle Andrew, the cabby and his horse Strawberry into the Wood and then into a dark, empty world. A voice begins to sing, and stars and a sun appear. The singer is a great Lion.

recap.title: The Founding of Narnia
recap.summary: The Lion's song brings up grass, trees and animals from the bare earth. The iron bar from London grows into a lamp-post, and Uncle Andrew starts scheming about how to make money from soil like this. The Lion chooses some of the animals and gives them the gift of speech.

recap.title: The First Joke and Other Matters
recap.summary: A jackdaw makes the first joke in the new world, and the Talking Beasts learn to laugh. The animals can't work out what Uncle Andrew is, and their attempts to look after him go comically wrong. Digory works up the courage to ask the Lion for something to cure his mother.

chapterQuestions.title: The Beginning of Uncle Andrew's Troubles
questions: Digory and Polly make up after their fight over the bell. Did the apology feel real to you?
Uncle Andrew is frightened of the Queen and flattered by her at the same time. What does that say about him?
Why does Lewis play this chapter mostly for laughs after the horror of Charn?

chapterQuestions.title: What Happened at the Front Door
questions: The Queen's magic fails in our world but her strength doesn't. Is she more or less frightening in London?
Aunt Letty stands up to her. What did you make of Aunt Letty?
Digory waits at the door to fix his mistake. Is this where he starts to grow up?
How does the chaos at the front door read to you: comedy, danger, or both?

chapterQuestions.title: The Fight at the Lamp-Post
questions: Digory grabs the Queen's ankle and takes her along. Brave, reckless, or both?
The cabby and his horse end up in another world by accident. Why do you think Lewis brings ordinary people along?
How did you picture the moment the singing begins in total darkness?

chapterQuestions.title: The Founding of Narnia
questions: Everyone hears the same song, yet reacts differently. Who reacts how, and why?
The iron bar becomes a lamp-post. What does that detail add?
Uncle Andrew looks at a new world and sees a money-making scheme. What does that tell us about him?
Which image from the creation scene has stuck with you most?

chapterQuestions.title: The First Joke and Other Matters
questions: Why might Lewis make a joke one of the first things a talking creature does?
The animals can't decide what Uncle Andrew is. Why can't he understand them either?
Digory wants to ask the Lion for help with his mother. What do you think he should ask for, and what might it cost him?

themes.title: Same song, different ears
themes.prompt: The cabby and Polly hear something beautiful; Uncle Andrew hears roaring he wants to ignore. Does what we notice depend on who we are?

themes.title: Wonder vs. greed
themes.prompt: Faced with a newborn world, Uncle Andrew thinks about profit. Where else in the book do characters miss wonder because they want to own things?

themes.title: Creation as music
themes.prompt: Lewis makes creation a song rather than a command. What does that change about how the world feels?

themes.title: Power out of its element
themes.prompt: In London the Queen is strong but her magic fails. What is Lewis saying about where her power really comes from?

themes.title: Ordinary goodness
themes.prompt: The cabby is one of the kindest people in the story. What makes him stand out next to Uncle Andrew?

themes.title: Hope and responsibility
themes.prompt: Digory brought the Queen into this world. Can he still ask for help for his mother? How do guilt and hope sit together?

context.title: Lewis and Tolkien
context.detail: Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien were close friends at Oxford and members of the Inklings writing group. Tolkien also imagined a world created through music, in the myth that opens The Silmarillion.

context.title: The lamp-post
context.detail: Readers of The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe will recognize this lamp-post. This book shows where it came from.

context.title: Written late, set first
context.detail: Published in 1955 as the sixth Narnia book, but set first in Narnia's history.

context.title: A dig at Uncle Andrew's kind
context.detail: Lewis often wrote against people who treat the world only as raw material. Uncle Andrew's money scheme in a newborn world is a sharp example.

guide.spoilerNote: Several of the people who arrive in Narnia in these chapters have bigger parts to play later in this book and in the series. Ask the group before going there.

the magician's nephew.about: C.S. Lewis's 1955 prequel to the Chronicles of Narnia, set in London around 1900. Digory and Polly get caught up in his uncle's experiment with magic rings and end up far from home, in other worlds. Published sixth in the series but set first in Narnia's history. 15 chapters.
